# R4 Digest — Provan, *1 and 2 Kings* (NIBC 1995), §26–§34

**Source:** Iain W. Provan, *1 and 2 Kings*, NIBC  
**Slice:** `.cache/provan-kings-reingest-2026-07-18/slices/R4_elijah_1943-2534.txt`  
**Raw lines:** 1943–2534  
**Scope:** §26 Elijah and the Drought (1 Kgs 17) · §27 Carmel (1 Kgs 18) · §28 Horeb (1 Kgs 19) · §29 Ahab vs Aram (1 Kgs 20) · §30 Naboth (1 Kgs 21) · §31 Ahab Dispatched / Micaiah (1 Kgs 22:1–40) · §32 Jehoshaphat & Ahaziah (1 Kgs 22:41–2 Kgs 1) · §33 Ascension & Elisha (2 Kgs 2) · §34 Excursus: Elijah in Canonical Context  
**Attribution:** All interpretive claims below are Provan’s (not wiki voice).

---

### C-R4-01 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Elijah bursts onto the Omride scene not first with dynastic doom (delayed until 21:21–24) but to dismantle Baal-worship introduced by Ahab, demonstrating that Baal is no more a god than Jeroboam’s calves; ch. 17’s drought is the context for Carmel’s climactic demonstration, proving the LORD (not Baal) controls life/death and fertility/infertility—as Elijah’s name itself proclaims.  
**Quote:** “His first task is to tackle the problem of the Baal-worship that Ahab has introduced into Israel (16:31–32), so as to demonstrate beyond all doubt that Baal is no more a god in any real sense than Jeroboam’s calves are. … It is thus the LORD, and not any other, who is God—as Elijah’s name (Hb. ʾēlîyāhû, ‘the LORD is God’) itself proclaims.”  
**Locus:** §26 intro; 1 Kgs 17:1–24 context (slice ~ll. 11).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-02 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Against Canaanite religion (Baal periodically submits to Mot, then revives to water the earth), Elijah’s living God can deny dew and rain while remaining present in judgment; infertility is the LORD’s presence in judgment, not divine absence in death (echoes Rev 11:6; 12:6).  
**Quote:** “It is the LORD, and not Baal, who brings fertility; it is the LORD’s presence in judgment that leads to infertility, rather than his absence in death (cf. the echoes of these verses in Rev. 11:6; 12:6).”  
**Locus:** §26 on 17:1–6 (slice ~ll. 13).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-03 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** At Kerith, God saves Elijah from Ahab/Jezebel yet sustains him by ravens—sovereign over the whole natural order; the word brings life, paralleling wilderness manna/meat (Exod 16), supplied even more liberally (bread and meat twice daily).  
**Quote:** “God is, however, able to provide for him; God controls not just the rain but the whole natural order, including the ravens (v. 4). God is ever present to speak the word (v. 2)—and the word brings life. And so, as the Israelites had once been the beneficiaries of God’s provision of bread and meat in the wilderness (Exod. 16 …), now Elijah also eats bread and meat—even more liberally than they.”  
**Locus:** §26 on 17:1–6 (slice ~ll. 13).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-04 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Elijah is sent to Zarephath of Sidon—the heartland of Baal worship (per 16:31)—so the LORD may show authority over foreign territory: drought, provision, and life-sustaining power there as in Israel; the widow is “commanded” as the ravens were.  
**Quote:** “God has decided to display power in a different way—in what 1 Kings 16:31 implies is the very heartland of the worship of Baal, the region of Sidon. … The LORD can bring drought to all and can disarm death and sustain life in even this area, as well as in Israel.”  
**Locus:** §26 on 17:7–16 (slice ~ll. 15).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-05 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** The widow acknowledges “the LORD lives” yet prepares to die; by feeding Elijah first against parental instinct she discovers Elijah’s God is alive and gives life—salvation within judgment at the foreign margin (cf. Matt 10:41).  
**Quote:** “The LORD lives (v. 12)—the woman is ready to acknowledge that; but she is preparing to die, for his living makes no practical difference to hers. … She does so (v. 15), and she and her son are blessed (cf. Matt. 10:41) as she discovers that Elijah’s God is alive and gives life.”  
**Locus:** §26 on 17:7–16 (slice ~ll. 15).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-06 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Raising the widow’s son is the ultimate test of the LORD’s authority vs Mot: can he act when death has “clamped tight its jaws”? Even the underworld is not barred to the LORD (Ps 139:7–12); life storms death’s towers (echoes Luke 7:11–17; Acts 9; 20; Heb 11:35).  
**Quote:** “It is one thing to rescue people from the jaws of death, but can he do anything when death has clamped tight its jaws and swallowed the victim up? … When faced by ‘Mot,’ must the LORD, like Baal, bow the knee? Elijah knows the answer … Even the underworld is not a place from which the LORD can be barred (Ps. 139:7–12).”  
**Locus:** §26 on 17:17–24 (slice ~ll. 17).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-07 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** The widow’s faith focuses on Elijah’s credentials as man of God more than on God himself—preparing for the public test when Elijah’s credentials will be measured against hundreds of rival “prophets.”  
**Quote:** “The widow’s response to this raising of her son from the dead is faith—but faith that is focused upon Elijah rather than upon God himself. It is Elijah’s credentials as a man of God (v. 24) that have been validated by the miracle… She is the first to know what will soon be public knowledge when Elijah’s credentials are put to the test in confrontation with hundreds of others who claim to be ‘prophets’ of a living god, but who are found wanting.”  
**Locus:** §26 on 17:17–24 (slice ~ll. 19).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-08 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim (additional notes):** Zarephath is taken up by Jesus in Luke 4:25–26 (sent also to Gentiles); echoes continue in the Canaanite/Phoenician woman’s daughter (Matt 15:21–28; Mark 7:24–30). The “command” of the widow may be indirectly causative (“I have ordained that…”). The boy’s raising hinges on prayer, not the body-stretching action.  
**Quote:** “Like Elijah, he implies, he has been sent, not (only) to Jews, but to Gentiles. … What is certain is that it is the prayer that is the crucial element in the whole scene.”  
**Locus:** §26 Additional Notes on 17:9, 17:18, 17:21 (slice ~ll. 41–47).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-09 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Ch. 18 is the “great battle of the war”: before rain returns, “all Israel” must know who is God via public confrontation of the LORD’s prophet with Baal’s prophets.  
**Quote:** “The time has now come for his reappearance on the main stage—for the great battle of the war, indeed. The drought is to end, but before it does it must be indisputable, not only to the widow of Zarephath but also to ‘all Israel,’ who is God.”  
**Locus:** §27 intro (slice ~ll. 69).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-10 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Ahab, like Baal, is impotent: he cannot find Elijah (even near Jezebel’s hometown) or grass for livestock; all initiative is God’s/Elijah’s. Obadiah (“servant of the LORD”) is caught between Ahab and Elijah; his feeding of prophets (ḵwl) parallels ravens and the widow.  
**Quote:** “Ahab, like Baal, is impotent. He can do nothing. He cannot find (Hb. mṣʾ) Elijah (v. 10); he is hard pressed, indeed, to find (Hb. mṣʾ) grass to keep the horses and mules alive (v. 5). All the initiative must come from God and God’s prophet.”  
**Locus:** §27 on 18:1–15 (slice ~ll. 71–73).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-11 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Ahab’s “troubler of Israel” (ʿḵr) echoes Achan (Josh 6–7): Ahab misunderstands the curse’s source—trouble is religious (abandoning LORD’s commands, worshiping Baals); Ahab, not Elijah, is the Achan of the narrative.  
**Quote:** “The trouble has religious roots—the abandonment of the LORD’s commands and the worship of the Baals … And it is Ahab, not Elijah, who is (ominously for him) the Achan of this narrative.”  
**Locus:** §27 on 18:16–19 (slice ~ll. 75).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-12 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Carmel settles before “all Israel” who is God; the people are not neutral—they waver but in practice worship Baal (dilapidated altar, v. 30); the ordeal of fire is to draw them back: “The god who answers by fire—he is God.”  
**Quote:** “They may waver between two opinions, but while they are weighing up the odds in their heads they are in practice worshiping Baal as their god (v. 24) and neglecting the worship of the LORD … The god who answers by fire—he is God (v. 24), and the people will be expected to follow him.”  
**Locus:** §27 on 18:20–24 (slice ~ll. 77).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-13 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Baalists’ “prophesying” is ecstatic spirit-possession (cf. Num 11; 1 Sam 10; 18–19)—here by a bad influence, “prophesy by Baal” (Jer 23:13; cf. lying spirits of 1 Kgs 22); Elijah is empowered by the Spirit of the LORD (18:12, 46; cf. Acts 8:39). Result: “no voice; no answer; no attentiveness.”  
**Quote:** “In the present passage, of course, it is certainly not a good influence that is in view: these men ‘prophesy by Baal’ (Jer. 23:13; cf. further the ‘lying spirits’ of 1 Kgs. 22:1–28). Elijah, on the other hand, is one empowered by the Spirit of the LORD (vv. 12, 46; cf. Acts 8:26–40, esp. v. 39).”  
**Locus:** §27 on 18:25–29 (slice ~ll. 79–81).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-14 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim (Carmel theophany):** Elijah rebuilds the LORD’s altar with twelve stones (true identity of Israel), saturates the sacrifice so only divine fire can explain combustion, and simply prays—no dance, shout, or mutilation. The fire of the LORD consumes sacrifice, stones, and soaking soil; people confess “The LORD—he is God!” and execute the Baal prophets (Achan pattern).  
**Quote:** “Having done all this, Elijah simply prays. No dancing, or shouting, or self-mutilation—simply a prayer. … The fire of the LORD falls—and it consumes not only the sacrifice but everything else around it, whether inflammable stones or soaking soil (v. 38). The LORD—he is God!”  
**Locus:** §27 on 18:30–40 (slice ~ll. 83).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-15 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Post-Carmel meal for Ahab parallels Exod 24 (twelve-stone altar; see God; eat and drink); Elijah races Ahab to Jezreel in the LORD’s power and wins—comprehensive dominance matching victory over Baal’s prophets; Ahab is as impotent as his god.  
**Quote:** “He is as impotent as the god he worships. Elijah’s ‘win’ over him is as comprehensive as his ‘win’ over the prophets of Baal.”  
**Locus:** §27 on 18:41–46 (slice ~ll. 85).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-16 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim (notes):** Asherah’s 400 prophets and Jezebel do not appear at Carmel—absent threats that remain after ch. 18; Elijah underestimates residual female/Asherah opposition. Hb. psḥ links people’s “hobbling” at the crossroads to Baalists hobbling around the altar. Fire/lightning contest may echo extrabiblical Baal claims (Bronner); high-place repair is tolerated vs idolatry (altar then consumed). Elijah’s run to Jezreel suggests he thinks the war is over—a “misjudgment” (only two verses before flight).  
**Quote:** “Elijah has dealt decisively with the men on the mountain; but what of the women, who were never involved in the proceedings? Ahab has been brought to submission, Baal shown to be no god; but what of Jezebel and Asherah? … The fact that he remains there for only two verses (19:1–2) before leaving again is testimony to the enormity of his misjudgment.”  
**Locus:** §27 Additional Notes on 18:19, 18:21, 18:24, 18:30, 18:45 (slice ~ll. 111–131).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-17 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Ch. 19 reveals Jezebel, not Ahab, as the true “general”; winning a battle is not winning the war. Ahab reports; Jezebel immediately vows to make Elijah’s life like the slain prophets—credible given her track record.  
**Quote:** “Yet there have been several hints in the narrative thus far that it is the queen, and not the king, who is the real general of the opposing forces. She will not be so easily cowed as her husband … That realization will send him into retreat, both physical and mental, as victory becomes defeat.”  
**Locus:** §28 intro; 19:1–2 (slice ~ll. 151–153).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-18 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Elijah’s flight is not by the word of the LORD (absent until v. 9’s question; then command to go back north, v. 15). Shocked by evidence-impervious Jezebel, he reacts to circumstances, seeks death under a broom tree—“Enough!”  
**Quote:** “but the ‘word of the LORD’ is, in fact, conspicuous by its absence here (contrast 17:2, 8; 18:1). It will not reappear until verse 9. There it will take the form of a question that makes it clear that, although the LORD has helped Elijah along the way, the journey was not of divine initiative.”  
**Locus:** §28 on 19:3–5 (slice ~ll. 155–157).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-19 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** God sends a malʾāk (messenger/angel) vs Jezebel’s; gentler than Jonah’s treatment, leading Elijah from anti-hero path back to faith. Food after “Enough!” (raḇ) then food so he will have enough (raḇ) for Horeb—forty days/nights recalling wilderness and Moses’ sojourn.  
**Quote:** “Food was God’s response when, at the end (as he thought) of his journey, Elijah cried ‘Enough!’; now food is provided a second time so that he will genuinely have enough—to complete his journey! … Is he to be servant Moses or stubborn Israel when he gets there, this runaway, self-pitying prophet?”  
**Locus:** §28 on 19:5–9 (slice ~ll. 159–161).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-20 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Elijah’s Horeb speech is selectively amnesiac—apostasy and casualties only, not restored faith, rebuilt altar, or slain Baal prophets; one woman becomes plural “they.” He needs to remember Carmel’s God of wind/earthquake/fire and regain perspective between self-loathing and self-importance.  
**Quote:** “But what of the Israelites restored to faith (18:39); the altar rebuilt (18:30–32); the prophets of Baal killed … with the sword (19:1)? Elijah’s memory is selective indeed. The resistance of one woman has in Elijah’s mind turned massive victory into overwhelming defeat … Somewhere between exaggerated self-loathing and exaggerated self-importance … there is a quiet place where Elijah must rest content with who he is and what he has done.”  
**Locus:** §28 on 19:9–12 (slice ~ll. 163).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-21 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim (still small voice):** Horeb/Sinai also teaches something new: Carmel emphasized spectacular fire; here God is not in wind, earthquake, or fire but in a gentle whisper (qôl demāmâh daqqâh). Elijah must realize there is more to the LORD than fire.  
**Quote:** “The emphasis at Carmel had been on God’s spectacular ways and particularly on his use of fire. The emphasis in verses 11–12, however, is upon God’s quiet ways. He is not to be found in the spectacular elements of the storm outside the cave (wind … earthquake … fire). He reveals himself on this occasion in a gentle whisper. Elijah needs to remember the past, but he also needs to realize that there is more to the LORD than fire.”  
**Locus:** §28 on 19:9–12; Additional Note 19:12 (slice ~ll. 165, 201).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-22 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** The demonstration seems to pass Elijah by: same self-pitying answer to the repeated question; he stays in the cave despite “Go out and stand…,” cloak over face—committed to “not seeing” like Jezebel. Privileged like Moses to see (Exod 33), he remains like Jonah: slow/unwilling to understand.  
**Quote:** “Privileged like Moses to see (Exod. 33:12–23), he remains steadfastly like Jonah: slow to understand. … He seems as committed to ‘not seeing’ as Jezebel was in 19:1–2.”  
**Locus:** §28 on 19:13–18 (slice ~ll. 167).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-23 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim (recommission):** The whisper’s point is disclosed by new instructions—anoint Hazael, Jehu, Elisha: final victory via political process and others’ efforts, not Elijah’s spectacular solo campaign; Carmel is one event in a series beyond his lifetime. Strategy always included quiet providence (still small voice only marginally noisier than Baal’s no-voice) and the 7,000 remnant (cf. Rom 11:1–6). Elijah must be part of the plan, not the plan itself—go north to Damascus, not south in despair.  
**Quote:** “Victory will come, in other words, as a result of political process—not through obviously spectacular demonstrations of divine power. … God has other ways of working—some of which make Elijah’s God seem almost as nonexistent as Baal (a still small ‘voice’ being only marginally noisier than no ‘voice’ at all …). … From the beginning it had involved the gentle but devastating whisper as well as the all-consuming fire … Elijah must be content with being part of the plan and not the plan itself.”  
**Locus:** §28 on 19:13–18 (slice ~ll. 169).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[elisha]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-24 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Elijah’s response is less than wholehearted: enlists Elisha as attendant but no “anointing” of Elisha, and he never meets/anoints Hazael or Jehu (Elisha will arrange Jehu). Elisha, by contrast, abandons livelihood (burns oxen/equipment), “runs” as Elijah once did; name points to the new era—“God saves” after Elijah’s day established “the LORD is God.”  
**Quote:** “Elijah has all but had his day—the day when it was established that ‘the LORD is God’ (18:39). The new era belongs to Elisha: ‘God saves.’”  
**Locus:** §28 on 19:19–21 (slice ~ll. 171–173).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[elisha]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-25 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim (notes):** Anointing Elisha / preparing the way is picked up in the NT for John the Baptist (Matt 11; 17; Mark 9; Luke 1; Mal 4:5); John designates Jesus as successor; Jesus = “the LORD saves,” as Elisha = “God saves.” Elisha’s parental kiss vs Baal-kiss (allegiance/abandonment); Luke 9:57–62 alludes with the plow. šrṯ “attendant” leaves succession ambiguous (Joshua//Moses vs Abishag/servant).  
**Quote:** “The idea that Elijah prepares the way for God’s kingdom rather than bringing it in himself is picked up in the NT in reference to John the Baptist … and the name Jesus means, of course, ‘the LORD saves,’ as Elisha means ‘God saves.’”  
**Locus:** §28 Additional Notes on 19:16, 19:20, 19:21 (slice ~ll. 203–207).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[elisha]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-26 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Ch. 20 underlines ch. 19: Elijah is not the only servant left; quiet ways continue before 19:17’s events. Ahab knows the LORD is God yet acts otherwise—Aphek’s Jericho-like victory followed by Achan/Saul-like failure; threat becomes explicit toward death in ch. 22.  
**Quote:** “Elijah is not the only servant of God left, in spite of what he has claimed (19:10, 14), and the quiet ways of God must take their course yet a while before the events that 19:17 speaks of come to pass. … Ahab is the ‘troubler of Israel,’ the Achan and the Saul of the northern monarchy. He knows that the LORD is God, but he acts in ways that belie this.”  
**Locus:** §29 intro (slice ~ll. 227).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-27 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Prophetic good news to Ahab (victory over Aram) is holy-war echo of past promises; purpose is exodus-like “then you will know that I am the LORD.” Aramean “gods of the hills” theology is false—the LORD acts in hills (ch. 18) and anywhere (ch. 17). Aphek wall falls Jericho-like.  
**Quote:** “As in chapter 18 (cf. vv. 30–39), the past is recalled to remind Israel that the LORD is still the same God and Israel still the same people. … the LORD is the only real God there is, and can be active both in the hills (1 Kgs. 18) and anywhere else (1 Kgs. 17).”  
**Locus:** §29 on 20:13–21, 20:22–25, 20:26–34 (slice ~ll. 233–239).  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-28 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Sparing Ben-Hadad for profit is Achan/ḥrm violation (like Saul, 1 Sam 15); Ahab tricked into self-judgment; life and kingship forfeit. Prophetic disguise (ḥpś) prefigures Ahab’s failed battlefield disguise (22:30)—disguises succeed only when God ordains.  
**Quote:** “Like Saul, Ahab has released a king whom God had determined should die (Hb. ḥrm, v. 42; cf. 1 Sam. 15:17–24). His life is therefore forfeit … For God is the prime mover behind all that happens to mortal beings, and disguises only succeed when God ordains it so.”  
**Locus:** §29 on 20:35–43 (slice ~ll. 241–243).  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-29 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim (Naboth justice):** Naboth’s refusal rests on land as inheritance under God (Lev 25:23; Josh 13)—not for perpetual sale. Ahab’s “vegetable garden” (gan-yārāq) alludes to Deut 11:10’s Egypt vs promised land; replacing vineyard (Israel-as-vine imagery) symbolizes making Israel like Egypt; idolatry and ethics are two sides of one coin—covetousness leads to false witness, murder, theft (Exod 20).  
**Quote:** “Ahab’s desire to replace a vineyard with a vegetable garden is meant to be seen as symbolic of a deeper desire. This is a king who wants to make Israel like Egypt … Worship and ethics are but two sides of the same coin, so far as the OT is concerned … Abandonment of God … inevitably leads to abandonment of righteousness.”  
**Locus:** §30 on 21:1–3 (slice ~ll. 309–311).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-30 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Jezebel drives the judicial murder: corrupted elders/nobles, two scoundrel witnesses (Deut 19), stoning outside the city. Passive Ahab is as blameworthy as active Jezebel; Elijah announces blood/dogs judgment on Ahab, Jezebel, and house like Jeroboam/Baasha for provoking the LORD and causing Israel to sin.  
**Quote:** “note that he is as much to blame in his passivity as is Jezebel in her activity … Ahab’s house is to suffer the same fate as the houses of Jeroboam and Baasha (v. 22 …), because Ahab has, like them, provoked the LORD to anger and caused Israel to sin.”  
**Locus:** §30 on 21:4–14, 21:15–24 (slice ~ll. 313–315).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-31 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Ahab is the worst of kings (Baal added to Jeroboam’s sin) yet penitent response delays house-disaster to his son’s days; sins so bad that lifetime house-judgment was expectable—humbling returns him to “normal” sinner timetable.  
**Quote:** “Presumably we are to take it that Ahab’s sins were so very bad that he could have expected judgment on his house in his lifetime. Now, however, he has humbled himself, and thus he is to be treated as a normal, rather than a spectacular, sinner.”  
**Locus:** §30 on 21:25–29 (slice ~ll. 317).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-32 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim (note on 21:19):** māqôm construct can mean “instead of” not “in the place where”—so 22:38’s Samaria pool fulfillment need not contradict Jezreel: “Instead of dogs licking up Naboth’s blood, dogs will lick up your blood—yes, yours!”  
**Quote:** “We should translate: ‘Instead of dogs licking up Naboth’s blood, dogs will lick up your blood—yes, yours!’”  
**Locus:** §30 Additional Note on 21:19 (slice ~ll. 343).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-33 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim (Micaiah / true prophecy):** Third prophet brings Ahab’s death at Ramoth Gilead. Assembly of ~400 “prophets” echoes Carmel’s missing Asherah prophets and 18:20’s phrasing; Jehoshaphat seeks a prophet of the LORD—authors imply majority are false leftovers from Carmel; one true prophet vs many false.  
**Quote:** “Once again a single true prophet is set against a large number of false prophets—by implication the very prophets ‘left over’ from that Carmel narrative. We already suspect, therefore, that this majority is not speaking the truth—that it is the one man who never prophesies anything good (v. 8) whose word will prove trustworthy.”  
**Locus:** §31 on 22:6–8 (slice ~ll. 369).

### C-R4-34 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Micaiah first echoes the false message (testing), then reveals the heavenly council: a lying spirit entices Ahab via the court prophets (cf. Ezek 14; Saul’s spirit, 1 Sam 16). Sheep without shepherd (Zech 13; Matt 9:36); people return bešālôm, Ahab will not. Prophecy is not under human control: “I can tell him only what the LORD tells me.”  
**Quote:** “The LORD has decreed disaster for Ahab at Ramoth Gilead (v. 23), and his plan to entice the king to his death there (v. 20) involves precisely those prophets whom Ahab first summoned into his presence … They are being influenced by a lying spirit (vv. 21–23 …).”  
**Locus:** §31 on 22:9–14, 22:15–25 (slice ~ll. 371–373).  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-35 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Ahab’s rational choice of 400 over Micaiah still ends in divinely aimed random arrow; disguise (learned from the wounded prophet) cannot thwart judgment—Jehoshaphat saved by shout; Ahab dies. Dogs/prostitutes at the pool recall Deut 23:17–18 idolatry (keleḇ/zônâ)—poetic justice for Naboth and whole career. Ahab is Saul not David; dynasty must fall.  
**Quote:** “An arrow shot at random flies unerringly to its divinely ordained target (v. 34) … Ahab’s attempted deception of the LORD has failed. It was the only possible outcome. … He has fed the people idolatry, and now he is consumed by it. … Ahab is Saul and not David.”  
**Locus:** §31 on 22:26–40 (slice ~ll. 375–383).

### C-R4-37 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Jehoshaphat is pious Davidic king (right in LORD’s eyes; removes shrine prostitutes; peace with Israel) yet high places remain; Solomonic pretensions (Edom; Tarshish ships at Ezion Geber) collapse—ships wrecked, refuses Israelite partners; days of humbling not glory (11:39). Ahaziah walks in Jeroboam’s/Baal ways; two-year reign fits doomed-house pattern.

### C-R4-38 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim (fire from heaven):** Injured Ahaziah consults Baal-Zebub of Ekron; LORD’s malʾāk sends Elijah with death oracle. Captains’ coercion meets Carmel’s God: fire from heaven consumes two fifties; third captain’s respect spares him. Oracle stands; king dies. Dynasty not yet blood-purged—Jehoram brother is another “son of Ahab”; delay not failed prophecy.  
**Quote:** “The peremptory instructions of verses 9 and 11, therefore, meet with a fierce response, as Ahaziah comes to terms with the reality of the God of Carmel, who can send fire from heaven to consume his captains (vv. 10 and 12; cf. 1 Kgs. 18:38). … We are dealing, then, not with failure of prophecy, but with another delay.”  
**Locus:** §32 on 2 Kgs 1:1–18 (slice ~ll. 443–445).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-39 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim (notes):** Baal-Zebub (“lord of the flies”) may corrupt Baal-Zebul; some Gospel MSS “Beelzebub” for Satan link OT Baal to NT demonology (cf. Carmel possession). Elijah’s “owner of hair” + leather belt → John Baptist’s dress (Matt 3:4; Mark 1:6). Fire judgment; Rev 11:1–6’s two prophets stop rain and kill with fire (Elijah + Moses). Chronology of Jehoram succession may imply Judean coregency.  
**Quote:** “The figure of Elijah appears to stand behind the representation of the two prophets in Rev. 11:1–6, who stop the rain and kill with fire those who try to harm them … Both Matt. (3:4) and Mark (1:6) portray John the Baptist (as ‘Elijah’) wearing both this kind of garment and a leather belt.”

### C-R4-40 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim (ascension setup):** Elijah’s days numbered since 19:15–18; ch. 2 transfers mantle—fire down in ch. 1 becomes fire up in ch. 2. Elijah repeatedly tries to leave Elisha though succession is “today”—possible further reluctance to God’s future plans; Elisha’s commitment (not Elijah’s leadership) decides the outcome.  
**Quote:** “As Elijah has called fire down from heaven in chapter 1, so in chapter 2 he will be lifted in fire up to heaven, and Elisha will be authenticated as one who stands in true succession to him as a prophet of the LORD. … Is this further testimony of Elijah’s reluctance to adopt God’s plans for the future (cf. 1 Kgs. 19:13–21)?”

### C-R4-41 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim (double portion):** Jordan crossing recalls Moses at the Sea; Elisha asks a firstborn’s double portion of spirit (not land)—receives if he sees the departure. He repeats the water-parting: Joshua to Elijah’s Moses; name-parallels (“God saves” / “the LORD saves”) invite reading the two successions together.  
**Quote:** “Elisha then requests what an eldest son would expect of a father (cf. v. 12) as his inheritance: a double portion (cf. Deut. 21:15–17). In this case it is not land that he has in mind, but spirit … proving himself to be Joshua to Elijah’s Moses … It is significant here that the names Elisha and Joshua are so similar in meaning (‘God saves’; ‘the LORD saves’).”

### C-R4-42 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Sons of the prophets bow to Elisha yet search for Elijah—only Elisha “sees” the ascent (ʿlh haššāmayîm); they may think Spirit relocated him (18:12) or seek a corpse for burial (clothes torn as mourning). Authorial ʿlh vs characters’ lqḥ guards the mystery: death or translation never resolved.  
**Quote:** “Whether that ‘taking up’ is itself a kind of death or simply translation to a different sort of life is never resolved by the narrative. … The authorial ‘taken up’ (Hb. ʿlh, vv. 1, 11) is distinctive language … that guards the mystery at the heart of the event and does not allow us easy answers.”  
**Locus:** §33 on 2:15–18 (slice ~ll. 507–513).

### C-R4-43 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Elisha authenticated by blessing (Jericho’s bad water under Joshua’s curse shadow) and curse (Bethel youths mauled by bears—disrespect for prophet = risk of retribution). Trip to Carmel then Samaria: ready to resume the Baal war. Chariot(s) of fire = divine army (seen at Dothan later); “My father! … chariots and horsemen of Israel!” Mantle permanently Elisha’s.  
**Quote:** “With the two concluding stories of the chapter we leave behind uncertainties about the fate of Elijah … and concentrate upon what is clear … that Elisha has indeed taken his place. He is an authentic prophet—a man able both to bless and to curse in the LORD’s name (cf. Moses in Deut. 28). … His prophetic credentials having been established, he is now ready to pick up where Elijah left off in the war against Baal.”  
**Locus:** §33 on 2:19–25; Additional Note 2:11–12 (slice ~ll. 515–517, 547–549).

### C-R4-44 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim (Excursus portrait):** Elijah is a mighty crisis prophet of faith and courage (1 Kgs 17–18) yet flawed (like all biblical heroes bar one): retreats under unexpected opposition, unwilling to hear the divine redefinition as one servant among many; after Horeb still serves (21; 2 Kgs 1) but shows reluctance/disobedience at succession points (19:19–21; 2:1–10). Like Moses (incl. “dying” east of Jordan) and like Jonah (grudging, disobedient).  
**Quote:** “He was also, however, as all biblical heroes of the faith (bar one) are ultimately shown to be, a flawed character. … He did well when life went the way he expected. He was not so good at dealing with disappointment; he was certainly not prepared to smooth the way for others. In many ways he was similar to Moses … but he was also somewhat like Jonah (1 Kgs. 19), the grudging, disobedient servant of God.”  
**Locus:** §34 Excursus opening (slice ~ll. 575).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[elisha]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-45 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim (Excursus — Elijah & Jesus):** Unlike Solomon, Elijah appears “in person” at the Transfiguration with Moses and Jesus; main point across Gospels: Jesus is greater than both mountain-meeting predecessors. Elijah still functions typologically of Jesus (explicit Luke 4:24–26 Gentiles; implicit: angels in wilderness, opposing Baal-Zebub/possession, provision/healing miracles, ascension—Acts 1:2).  
**Quote:** “The main point in all three, however, appears to be that Jesus is greater than both Moses and Elijah, those others privileged to meet with God on a mountain. … In all these ways and more, the NT portrait of Jesus is building on the portrait of Elijah in Kings.”  
**Locus:** §34 (slice ~ll. 577).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-46 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim (Excursus — John the Baptist / Malachi):** Most Gospel connection is John, via Elijah’s preparatory role (1 Kgs 19:15–18 → Mal 4:1–6): prepares for final victory over darkness. John dressed like Elijah; identified as Elijah-to-come by angel (Luke 1:11–17) and Jesus (Matt 11; 17; Mark 9). Gospels reject popular literal-return theory (ambiguity of 2 Kgs 2 + Enoch Gen 5:24 / Heb 11:5); Transfiguration places “real” Elijah on the mountain so John is figurative Elijah—explains John’s denial (John 1:21). Same figurative pattern for Rev 11 witnesses (Elijah + Moses patterning).  
**Quote:** “Here it is Elijah’s preparatory role that is in view (1 Kgs. 19:15–18, picked up in Mal. 4:1–6). He prepares the way for God’s final victory over the powers of darkness. … the transfiguration narrative in Matthew and Mark makes it quite clear that John is ‘Elijah’ only in some figurative sense. This may explain John’s own denial that he is Elijah (John 1:19–34). In one sense he is, in another he is not.”  
**Locus:** §34 (slice ~ll. 579).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[elisha]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-47 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim (Excursus — moral/theological afterlife):** Elijah also models “someone just like us”: remnant (Rom 11), faith (Heb 11:32–39), prayer (Jas 5:13–18). Provan adds lessons on perspective, humility, willingness to be part of God’s plan rather than the plan itself (Matt 3:11–15; 11:11; 20:20–27; John 3:27–30; 1 Cor 3; Phil 1). Success and failure both instruct.  
**Quote:** “On the basis of my own reading of the Elijah story, I may also suggest that there are things to be learned from him regarding having a sense of perspective about one’s life of service; regarding the need for humility; regarding willingness to be part of God’s plan, rather than to be the plan itself … Both in his success and in his failure Elijah is a helpful teacher.”  
**Locus:** §34 closing (slice ~ll. 581).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R4-48 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim (synthesis — salvation within judgment):** Across 17–2 Kgs 2 Provan frames Elijah as agent of the living God’s life-giving power inside a judgment context (drought, death, fire, dynastic doom): provision and resurrection at Kerith/Zarephath; Carmel fire that both vindicates and purges; Horeb’s recommission of a long war of whisper and politics; Naboth’s justice-oracle; Micaiah’s true word amid lying spirits; fire on captains; double-portion succession so the Baal war continues. Judgment and salvation are not alternatives but coordinated modes of the LORD’s kingship.  
**Quote:** “That he is indeed the living and ever-present God who is sovereign over creation is, in fact, revealed in the story that follows in which he is able to sustain and even to restore life in the midst of death.” / “From the beginning it had involved the gentle but devastating whisper as well as the all-consuming fire, the quiet ways of God’s normal providence as well as the noiser ways of miraculous intervention.”  
**Locus:** §26 on 17:1–6; §28 on 19:13–18 (slice ~ll. 13, 169)—composite thesis spanning block.  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[elisha]], [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-49 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Saul typology saturates the Ahab narrative (troubler; prophetic opposition; failure to kill ḥrm-devoted enemy; spirit from God; disguise before death)—so Ahab lacks Davidic exemption (2 Sam 7:14–16); northern dynasties fall like the reed in the water (14:14–16).  
**Quote:** “Indeed, the echoes of the story of Saul (among those of many other stories) are everywhere to be heard in Ahab’s tale … Like Jeroboam, he was not of David’s house and he was not, therefore, exempt from being treated like Saul (2 Sam. 7:14–16).”  
**Locus:** §31 closing synthesis (slice ~ll. 383); cf. §27 note 18:17; §29 (slice ~ll. 109, 227).  
**Targets:** [[david]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-50 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** “All Israel” at Carmel still means twelve tribes (not ten): twelve stones, twelve water-dousings (four jars × three); Israel remains Israel despite political schism—echoes Exod 24 and Josh 4.  
**Quote:** “It is interesting to note that ‘all Israel’ is conceived in this passage, as earlier in Kings, to consist of twelve tribes and not ten. Israel is still Israel, whatever the de facto political situation with regard to its mode of government may be.”  
**Locus:** §27 Additional Note on 18:30 (slice ~ll. 123–125).  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-51 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Elijah’s “I am the only one left” is partly strategy (odds 450:1) and partly false self-drama—Obadiah hid prophets; other prophets appear (20:35–43; 22); Horeb names 7,000. Selective memory fuels both despair and inflated centrality.  
**Quote:** “Whether the odds quoted here in v. 22 (450 to 1!) are entirely accurate, or simply part of this strategy, is unclear. He is certainly the only prophet of the LORD present, but is he the only prophet of the LORD left (cf. 18:4, 13; 20:35–43; 22:1–28)?”  
**Locus:** §27 Additional Note on 18:22; §28 on 19:9–12 (slice ~ll. 115, 163).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R4-52 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Numerical tissue unifies 1 Kgs 17–2 Kgs 2: fifties (fire on captains; witnesses of ascension/search); 400 prophets Carmel/Micaiah; 7,000 remnant/army; 32 kings/chariot commanders; forty-two mauled youths reappear at 2 Kgs 10:14—literary convention binding the prophetic block.  
**Quote:** “As in other parts of 1 Kgs. 17–2 Kgs. 2, numbers are apparently functioning as a way of holding separate narratives together as a unity. … In view of this and other examples of numerical linking, it seems noteworthy that the other larger number of this chapter—the ‘forty-two’ of v. 24—also reappears, in 2 Kgs. 10:14.”  
**Locus:** §33 Additional Note on 2:7; §31 Note 22:30 (slice ~ll. 543, 415).  
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[elisha]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]
